In the eye, toxoplasma primarily affects the retina and choroid, usually in the periphery.C
In immunocompromised patients, especially people living with HIV, Toxoplasma gondii can cause toxoplasmic meningoencephalitis.C
Toxoplasmosis is one of the TORCH infections that can cause congenital abnormalities through maternal to fetal transmission.C

background.definition: Toxoplasmosis is an infection caused by the single-celled parasite Toxoplasma gondii, which is transmitted through ingestion of undercooked, contaminated meat (particularly pork, lamb, and venison), contaminated water, or fecal-oral transmission via contaminated soil or cat feces. Most immunocompetent persons infected with T. gondii are asymptomatic or have mild flu-like symptoms. However, it can cause encephalitis or ocular disease in the immunocompromised and can also affect newborns who are infected through maternal-fetal transmission.

list.listitem: Estimated 400 to 4,000 cases of congenital toxoplasmosis occur each year in the United States.

Approximately 750 deaths are attributed to toxoplasmosis in the United States each year, of which 50% are believed to be caused by eating contaminated meat, making toxoplasmosis the third leading cause of foodborne deaths in that country.

Before antiretroviral therapy (ART) was available, the incidence of toxoplasmosis encephalitis (TE) was 33% in persons with advanced immunosuppression, seropositive for T. gondii, and not on prophylaxis.
Global prevalence ranges from 10% to 90%, with the highest prevalence in hot, humid climates such as Latin America and tropical Africa.

Analysis of National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) data shows a 13.2% prevalence in persons >6 years old in the United states in 2009 to 2010, which is a decline from the past two decades.
In one urban cohort of patients with advanced HIV, toxoplasmosis infection occurred at a rate of approximately 2 to 4 events per 100 person-years.
Global IgG seroprevalence for toxoplasmosis in pregnant women was 32.9% with the highest prevalence (45.2%) in the Americas and the lowest prevalence in the Western Pacific.
The prevalence of occular toxoplasmosis was found to be 0.37% among people living with HIV and 2% in the general population.
Toxoplasma gondii is a single-celled protozoan parasite that exists as oocysts, tachyzoites, and bradyzoites.

Oocysts are produced in the definitive host, animals in the family Felidae (which includes domestic cats) and is passed via stool to humans and other intermediate hosts where oocysts develop into rapidly multiplying tachyzoites that destroy tissue and spread the infection. Tachyzoites then develop into bradyzoites, which are tissue cysts which are located in muscle tissue of skeletal muscle, myocardium, brain tissue, and the eye in humans.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Eating raw oysters, clams, or mussels
Eating locally produced cured, dried, or smoked meat

list.listitem: Routine prenatal screening of pregnant women is not recommended in the United States. C
Upon initiation of care, persons infected with HIV with CD4 counts <200 cells/mm3 should be screened for anti-toxoplasma immunoglobulin G (IgG) antibodies.B
Primary prevention of congenital toxoplasmosis through prenatal education has not been shown to be effective.B

Pregnant women and persons living with HIV (PLWH) who are seronegative for anti-toxoplasma IgG antibodies should avoid eating raw or undercooked meat and shellfish, wash their hands after contact with raw meat or soil, and avoid changing cat litter boxes.

For primary prevention of toxoplasma encephalitis (TE) in Toxoplasma IgG positive PLWH with CD4 counts <100 cells/mm3, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) double strength (DS) daily is first line. Second-line therapies include TMP-SMX DS 3 times per week, TMP-SMX single strength daily, dapsone with pyrimethamine and leucovorin weekly, atovaquone ± pyrimethamine and leucovorin.

In patients with allogeneic hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation who are seropositive for Toxoplasma gondii before transplant, trimethoprim-sulfamethozazole prophylaxis for a least 6 months and weekly blood screening using quantitative PCR has been recommended by European guidelines (2022).

After completion of initial treatment for TE in PLWH, chronic maintenance therapy with consideration of dual coverage for Pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP) prophylaxis should be continued until the CD4 count is >200 cells/mm3 for at least 6 months.

Suspect toxoplasmosis in pregnant women in endemic areas with acute flu-like symptoms, newborns with retinochoroiditis, hydrocephalus or intracranial calcifications, and immunocompetent individuals with neurological symptoms. C
Serology, including IgM and IgG antibodies, is recommended for diagnosis of immunocompetent individuals. C

In immunocompromised patients with central nervous systems symptoms, characteristic brain imaging and/or polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing can be used for detection of T. gondii DNA in blood, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), ocular aqueous humor, and brochoalveolar lavage. C
See for an overview of recommended diagnostic tests for different clinical scenarios.

IgM antibodies to toxoplasmosis are often present 1 week after acute infection and may persist for months. IgG antibodies to toxoplasmosis are typically present 2 weeks after acute infection and persist for life.
See for interpretation of IgM and IgG serology.
PCR analysis can be utilized for detection of T. gondii in amniotic fluid, with overall sensitivity and specificity for detection of children born with toxoplasmosis of 92% and 100%, respectively.
CSF PCR testing has low sensitivity but high specificity for toxoplasma.

Histopathological criteria can diagnose toxoplasmic lymphadenitis with high sensitivity (100%), high specificity (97%), and high positive likelihood ratio (29) in patients for whom IgM serology results are not clearly diagnostic.
Brain MRI in patients with toxoplasmic encephalitis most commonly shows multiple ring enhancing lesions, which should be differentiated from lypmhoma.
On brain CT scan, toxoplasmosis was the most common intracranial lesion in patients living with HIV with CD4 counts <200 cells/μL.
summarizes interpretation of serology, and summarizes a suggested diagnostic and treatment approach to the patient.
Pyrimethamine-containing regimens are preferred for treatment of retinochoroiditis and encephalopathy. C
Limited evidence exists for treatment of pregnant women to prevent congenital toxoplasmosis. B
Supportive treatment is recommended for persons who are non-pregnant and immunocompetent.
Pyrimethamine, a folic acid antagonist, can cause suppression of the bone marrow, which can be reduced by also giving leucovorin

listitem.strong: Treatment of toxoplasmosis in immunocompetent pregnant women

list.listitem: No randomized controlled trials (RCTs) have been performed to determine if treatment during pregnancy is beneficial for reducing congenital transmission. .

Treatment may be considered during pregnancy with spiramycin, pyrimethamine with leucovorin and sulfadiazine, or azithromycin. Spiramycin is recommended for women diagnosed before 18 weeks gestation and infection of the fetus is not documented or suspected. Spiramycin reduces transmission to the fetus and is most effective if initiated within 8 weeks of seroconversion.

CDC guidance recommends pyrimethamine with leucovorin and sulfadiazine for 1 year is recommended based on cohort studies and expert opinion. Dosing is as follows: Pyrimethamine: 2 mg/kg / day orally, divided twice / day for the first 2 days; then from day 3 to 2 months (or 6 months if symptomatic) 1 mg/kg / day, orally, every day; then 1 mg/kg / day, orally, 3 times per week Sulfadiazine: 100 mg/kg / day, orally, divided twice / day Folinic acid (leucovorin): 10 mg, 3 times / week

Adults: CDC guidance recommends pyrimethamine 100 mg for 1 day as a loading dose, then 25 to 50 mg per day, plus sulfadiazine 2 to 4 grams daily for 2 days, followed by 500 mg to 1 gram dose four times per day, plus folinic acid (leucovorin) 5-25 mg with each dose of pyrimethamine. Patients should be treated for 4 to 6 weeks, followed by reevaluation of the patient’s condition.
Pediatric dosing: CDC guidance recommends pyrimethamine 2 mg/kg first day then 1 mg/kg each day, plus sulfadiazine 50 mg/kg two times per day, plus folinic acid (leucovorin) 7.5 mg per day.
Antibiotics are likely to reduce the risk of recurrent toxoplasma retinochoroiditis, but it is not clear that this results in better visual outcomes.
There is no evidence for or against use of steroids, in addition to antibiotics.
A 2021 systemic review and meta-analysis did not show a statistical difference in safety nor efficacy amond different treatment regimens for ocular toxoplasmosis.

A systematic review of case reports and case series found reports of successful treatment using intravitreal medications including anti-VEGF, antiparasitic and anti-inflammatory drugs. There are randomized trials and this should only be considered if other approaches have failed.

listitem.strong: Treatment of toxoplasmosis encephalitis (TE) in those with AIDS

list.listitem: Pyrimethamine with leucovorin and sulfadiazine or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole are first line for a minimum of 6 weeks. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole has comparable efficacy to first-line therapies, may be better tolerated, and can be useful in low resource settings due to lower cost. Second-line therapies include: (1) pyrimethamine + leucovorin + clindamycin, (2) atovaquone + pyrimethamine + leucovorin, (3) atovaquone + sulfadiazine, and (4) atovaquone alone.
Consider addition of corticosteroids to reduce cerebral mass effects or edema. Antiretroviral therapy may be initiated 2 to 3 weeks after the diagnosis of TE.
Immunocompetent individuals typically have full resolution of symptoms with no late sequelae. B
Prenatal treatment has not been shown to significantly reduce the risk of retinochoroiditis.B
In people with AIDS with TE, case fatality rates approaching 20% have been reported in those receiving treatment.B
The risk of congenital transmission of toxoplasmosis is highest with maternal seroconversion in the third trimester of pregnancy.

In a prospective cohort of 666 infants treated for maternal toxoplasmosis infection acquired during pregnancy, 17% had congenital toxoplasmosis, of whom 74% were asymptomatic and 26% had retinochoroiditis with rare neurological complications.B

A prospective study in France followed 646 children with congenital toxoplasmosis for a median of 12 years and found that 187 (29%) had at least 1 ocular lesion, with peak onset at 7 and 12 years of age. Early maternal infection and the presence of noocular signs at birth were associated with a higher risk of retinochoroiditis.

Pyrimethamine plus sulfadiazine treatment for 1 year of infants with congenital toxoplasmosis without neurologic disease resulted in normal cognitive, neurologic, and auditory outcomes, while infants with moderate or severe neurologic disease treated for 1 year resulted in normal neurologic and/or cognitive outcomes for >72% of children.
Up to 30% of children with treated for congenital toxoplasmosis develop retinochoroiditis.
Retinochoroiditis is more common in children with nonocular clinical manifestations of congenital toxoplasmosis.B
Children who have no retinochoroiditis detected before 4 months of age have a low probability of later development of retinochoroiditis.B
Approximately 25% of children with congenital retinochoroiditis can develop late-onset retinal lesions and have relapses many years after birth.
The mean recurrence rate for adults with retinochoroiditis after 3 years of follow-up was 49% for all patients (60 of 122 patients), with no differences between treated and untreated patients.

listitem.strong: Toxoplasmosis Encephalitis (TE) in Those with AIDS

list.listitem: Pyrimethamine-based treatment from studies before highly active retroviral therapy (HAART) shows relapse rates of 19%, with the relapse rate dropping to 11% in HAART era studies.
Severe disseminated toxoplasmosis requiring ICU admissions has a 82% 60-day mortality.
Allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplant recipients have the highest risk of mortality.
A systematic review found an association between T. gondi positivity and mild cognitive impairment, although it is not clear whether it was causal.
